title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F17
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 32 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Retrieve the ERA5 monthly mean geopotential at the 500 hPa pressure level over Europe for January 2023. Describe the main large-scale circulation patterns visible in the data.

answers.text:
The file geopotential_500hPa_2023_01.nc is a NetCDF file, which is not an image format. It contains geopotential data at the 500 hPa pressure level for Europe in January 2023.

Since I cannot process NetCDF files as images, I cannot visually describe the large-scale circulation patterns from this data. However, I can provide a textual description based on the data structure and typical meteorological patterns for January 2023 over Europe.

Typical Large-Scale Circulation Patterns in January 2023 over Europe:
• Blocking High Pressure: January 2023 was characterized by a strong and persistent blocking high-pressure system over the North Atlantic and western Europe. This led to a relatively stable and cold weather pattern across much of the continent.
• Jet Stream Position: The polar jet stream was positioned to the north of Europe, allowing cold Arctic air to remain confined to the north and keeping Europe relatively mild compared to other winters.
• Low Pressure Systems: There were fewer low-pressure systems over the central and eastern parts of Europe, which contributed to prolonged periods of clear skies and calm winds.
• Temperature Gradient: A strong temperature gradient existed between the cold Arctic air to the north and the relatively milder air over the Mediterranean, which influenced the movement of weather systems.

If you need a more detailed analysis or visualization of this data, you may need to use specialized climate data tools or software (e.g., Python with xarray, matplotlib, or GIS tools) to process and plot the NetCDF file.

Let me know if you'd like further assistance!

The issue has been resolved. Here is the visualization of the ERA5 monthly mean geopotential at 500 hPa over Europe for January 2023, along with a description of the large-scale circulation patterns:

Visualization Output
The plot has been saved as a PNG file at the following path:

era5_500hPa_geopotential_jan2023.png

Description of Large-Scale Circulation Patterns
The visualization reveals the following key features:

1. North Atlantic Ridge:
   • A ridge (positive geopotential anomaly) is visible over the North Atlantic, extending toward Western Europe. This ridge is associated with blocking patterns, which can lead to persistent weather regimes such as cold air outbreaks or prolonged dry conditions over Europe.

2. Trough Over Eastern Europe:
   • A trough (negative geopotential anomaly) is present over Eastern Europe or Scandinavia, indicating lower geopotential heights. This feature is linked to the advection of cold Arctic air into Eastern Europe and the Balkans.

3. Zonal Flow Over Central Europe:
   • A relatively zonal (west-to-east) flow is observed over Central Europe, reflecting strong westerly winds. This pattern is characteristic of the positive phase of the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), which brings mild and wet conditions to Northern Europe.

4. Mediterranean Anomalies:
   • The Mediterranean region may exhibit weak anomalies, but it is influenced by the positioning of the North Atlantic ridge and the Eastern European trough. If the trough extends southward, it can lead to cyclogenesis in the Mediterranean, resulting in stormy conditions.

5. Blocking Patterns:
   • The presence of a strong ridge over the North Atlantic or Western Europe can lead to blocking patterns, disrupting the typical westerly flow. This can result in prolonged cold spells or dry conditions over parts of Europe.

Summary
The ERA5 500 hPa geopotential height field for January 2023 reflects a dynamic wintertime circulation pattern, characterized by:
• A ridge over the North Atlantic,
• A trough over Eastern Europe,
• Zonal flow over Central Europe, and
• Potential blocking patterns influencing weather regimes.

Main Large-Scale Circulation Patterns in January 2023 (500 hPa Geopotential)
The 500 hPa geopotential height field is a key indicator of large-scale atmospheric circulation. Here’s a brief interpretation of typical patterns for January 2023 over Europe:

1. Ridges and Troughs:
   • Ridges (high geopotential heights) often indicate areas of descending air, stable conditions, and fair weather.
   • Troughs (low geopotential heights) are associated with ascending air, instability, and stormy conditions.
   • In January 2023, Europe likely experienced a mix of these features, with troughs over Western Europe (bringing stormy and wet conditions) and ridges over Eastern Europe or the Mediterranean (bringing drier and more stable conditions).

2. Zonal vs. Meridional Flow:
   • A zonal flow (west-to-east) is characterized by relatively straight, parallel height contours, often leading to mild but unsettled conditions in Europe.
   • A meridional flow (north-to-south or south-to-north) is indicated by amplified ridges and troughs, which can lead to extreme weather (e.g., cold snaps in Western Europe or warm spells in the north).
   • January 2023 likely featured a mix of zonal and meridional flow, with periods of both.

3. North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) Influence:
   • A positive NAO (stronger Icelandic Low and Azores High) typically results in a stronger zonal flow over Europe, with storm tracks directed toward Northern Europe.
   • A negative NAO (weaker pressure gradient) can lead to blocking patterns, with high pressure over Scandinavia or Greenland and cold air outbreaks over Europe.
   • For January 2023, the NAO was likely positive, given the prevalence of westerly flow and stormy conditions in Northern Europe.

4. Blocking Patterns:
   • If a strong ridge persisted over Western Europe or the North Atlantic, it could have led to blocking, causing prolonged cold or dry spells in parts of Europe.
